planting.note: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil; this diminutive European species resents soggy ground and is best tucked where excess winter moisture drains away.

directions: A true miniature among sedges, forming a tight evergreen tuft of narrow dark-green leaves finely edged in creamy white, native to limestone grasslands and open woodland edges across Europe. Performs best in partial to full shade alongside hostas and ferns, though it also tolerates sun if soil stays well drained, since it naturally grows on skeletal, fast-draining limestone sites. Its small scale suits rock gardens, container plantings, and the front of a shaded border where larger sedges would overwhelm it.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade.

directions: A low, cascading member of the EverColor series bred as a chimeral sport of 'Evergold' by Pat Fitzgerald at Fitzgerald Nurseries of Ireland, with leathery dark-green leaves banded by a wide, gleaming golden center stripe. Forms a non-spreading, well-behaved clump that holds its color year-round in mild climates and tolerates dry shade once established, making it useful under trees where irrigation is limited. Pairs well with its EverColor siblings or broad-leaved shade perennials in mixed containers and woodland edges.

planting.note: Plant in average to wet soil; tolerates standing water seasonally and is a strong choice for rain garden basins under tree cover.

directions: A statuesque native of wet meadows and streambanks across the northeastern and north-central United States and eastern Canada, emerging with silvery new growth in early spring before developing an upright, vase-shaped clump that relaxes into a mound as the season progresses. Produces sweeping brown-and-white flower spikes in May that have been likened to sprays of pipe cleaners, adding texture well beyond typical lawn-substitute sedges. Prefers part to full shade with medium to wet soil, making it well suited to rain gardens and the damp margins of woodland streams, though it tolerates full sun given enough moisture.

common_name: Straw Hat Pennsylvania Sedge (Showy-Flowered Oak Sedge)

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions 6-12 inches apart in well-drained to dry soil in partial to full shade; a slower spreader than the straight species, so allow extra time to fill in.

directions: A patented selection of native Pennsylvania sedge, discovered and bred by Brent Horvath from an open-pollinated seedling chosen for unusually showy spring flowering, with florets roughly three to four times larger than the wild species and seed heads that follow suit, giving the clump a frothy, straw-colored haze in April and May. Forms the same fine-textured, bright-green, semi-evergreen mat as the species but spreads more slowly by rhizome, making it easier to keep within bounds as a lawn substitute under oak and other deciduous trees. Thrives in dry to average shade with no mowing, fertilizer, or irrigation required once established.
